{"output": "151 159:

This was his first experience with death, but it would not be his last. In the years to come, Bob would lose his grandparents. His first wife. Both of his parents. And Bob never felt like Bob understood any of it. Death is a part of life Bob has never fully understood. Bob was not sure anyone does.

160:

But Bob remembered that dog. Bob remembered the weight of his head on his knee. The sound of his bark. The way he looked at him like Bob was the only person worth following.

161:

And Bob remembered that stretch of gravel road, the wind moving through his fur, and the terrible stillness of a body that no longer held its soul.

164:

In 1961, Bob was a young boy growing up in a world that was changing faster than anyone around him seemed to understand. The Space Race was accelerating. The Cold War pressed on. But for a nine-year-old, the biggest events happened at ground level, on the streets of his neighborhood and in the hallways of his school.

166:

But one day, without explanation, the friendship ended. His friend’s parents, succumbing to the pressures of a society still deeply divided by race, forced their son to disassociate from Bob. There was no argument, no fight, no falling-out between the boys. Just an absence. A desk that remained empty. A space in the routines of childhood where a friend had been.

167:

This was Bob’s first encounter with the ugly face of discrimination. It would not be his last. As he grew older, the Civil Rights Movement began to gain momentum. Television screens filled with images of sit-ins, protests, and marches. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was a landmark moment, but Bob understood even then that legislation alone could not change deeply ingrained attitudes. Discrimination and segregation persisted, not just against Black Americans but against other marginalized communities as well.

168:

Bob thought about this often. People discriminate against so many groups—Black, Jewish, Irish, Arab, Asian, Hispanic, fat people, gay people, trans people, women, immigrants, law enforcement, Native Americans, and others—he thought to himself. Why? Who is even left? This is crazy.

169:

Although a level of prejudice is ingrained in people who have been exposed to endemic discrimination all of their lives, Bob made a conscious decision early on: he would try to judge people by each person’s character, not by stereotyping. That lost friendship was a scar that taught him something no book ever could. The wound healed, but the lesson did not fade.

178:

The years of Bob's adolescence and young adulthood were among the most turbulent in American history — a period when the certainties of the 1950s shattered and a radically different nation emerged from the wreckage. For a boy in Michigan with his hands covered in sawdust and solder, the world outside the garage was transforming at a pace that must have felt, at times, impossible to keep pace with.

180:

By the time Bob entered high school in the mid-1960s, the postwar consensus had collapsed. The assassination of John F. Kennedy in 1963 had cracked something fundamental in the American psyche — a sense that history's arc bent toward progress, that the worst was behind them. What followed was a cascade of events that rewrote the nation's script: the escalation of the Vietnam War under Lyndon Johnson, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, the rise of the counterculture, the assassinations of Martin Luther King Jr. and Robert Kennedy in 1968, and the riots that consumed American cities in the summers of those years.

182:

The Vietnam War, which loomed over Bob's senior year when his draft number came up low, was the defining trauma of his generation. It was a war fought not by a mobilized nation but by a lottery, a conflict that fell unevenly on the working class and the poor. The draft deferment Bob received through his electronics training was not heroism — it was survival, a practical decision made by a young man who understood that the alternative meant rice paddies and body bags. More than one hundred thousand draft-age Americans fled to Canada. Thousands more went to prison. The fifty-eight thousand names on the Vietnam Memorial in Washington represent only the dead; the wounded — physically and psychologically — numbered in the millions.

184:

But the decade was not defined by war alone. It was also a time of extraordinary technological acceleration. Integrated circuits, invented in 1958, were beginning to transform every industry. The minicomputer revolution made computing accessible to universities and businesses for the first time. When Bob encountered the PDP-8 at Michigan State, he was touching the leading edge of a wave that would crest into the personal computer revolution of the 1970s and 80s. The Apollo program reached its zenith with the moon landing in 1969, fulfilling the promise John F. Kennedy had made at the dawn of the decade. Bob watched Neil Armstrong step onto the lunar surface, and he understood — perhaps for the first time — that the skills he was developing in electronics labs and physics classrooms could connect him to something genuinely historic.

188:

Bob built a boat in his father's garage during these years. It was an act of creation in a time of destruction — a small rebellion against the chaos of the era, a reminder that building things mattered even when the world seemed determined to tear itself apart. He did not know it then, but the discipline he learned in that garage — measuring twice, cutting once, persisting through failure — would carry him through everything that followed.

192:

You know how some places just feel different the moment you walk in? Like the air itself has a different weight? That's how the garage felt. If the dinner table was where his father's Navy training went to die—rigid, oppressive, all about obedience—the garage was where he became someone else entirely. Someone Bob actually wanted to be around.

193:

Bob was ten. Maybe eleven. Bob didn't remember exactly, but Bob remembered the smell. Glue, sharp and sweet—that distinctive petroleum tang that clung to your scent. Balsa bits everywhere. Silence that wasn't awkward, just companionable. This was the smell of possibility. Of things being built instead of broken. Of knowledge passing from one pair of hands to another without a single order being given.

194:

His father let him use a scroll saw one afternoon. Heavy thing, cast iron, probably made back in the '40s. "Show you something," he said. Not "Do this." Not "Pay attention." Just show you something. He took a board—pine, maybe a foot long—and demonstrated. One careful cut, shaving off a ribbon of wood so thin you could almost see through it. "Your turn." Bob flinched, waiting for the yell, the criticism, the "for Christ's sake, Bobby" Bob knew so well from dinner. He adjusted his grip. Moved his left hand forward. "Feel it," he said. And here's the thing—his voice was different in the garage. Softer. Like he was talking to the wood as much as to him. "The saw blade will tell you what it wants if you listen."

195:

That was a different language. Not the Navy language of commands and compliance. Something older. The wood had grain, and if you went against it, you'd feel the resistance before the tool even bit. You'd hear it in the change of sound, feel it in your hands through the plane's body. Competence mattered more than compliance here. Understanding trumped obedience. The garage had its own rules, its own hierarchy, and it operated on a currency Bob was starting to understand. Skill. Not rank. Not volume. Just... could you make the thing work? Could you make it well.

197:

The project that would eat up a year of his life sat in the middle of that garage like a promise. Sixteen feet of wooden boat and a trailer built from plans Bob had ordered from some magazine—Popular Mechanics, Bob thought, though it could have been Mechanix Illustrated. Both had those glossy covers with guys in work shirts holding tools. It was ambitious. Probably too ambitious for a boy in school. But that was part of what made it matter.

199:

The frame went up first—impossibly fragile on its own until the ribs went in. They curved like whale bones, giving the structure shape and strength. Bob learned to steam-bend wood. You wrap wood in wet rags and heat them over a washtub of boiling water until they become pliable, then bend them around forms before they cool and set. The physics fascinated him, though Bob didn't have the words then. How heat defeated the structural memory of cellulose. How water acted as a plasticizer. How the wood would hold its new shape once dry, like it had forgotten it was ever straight.

200:

His father was an intuitive engineer. A man who understood forces and stresses through feel and experience. He could look at a structure and know if it was sound, sense when a joint was weak or a line was true. But even then, Bob wanted to know why. Bob pored over those plans, studying the drawings, trying to understand the principles behind the design. Why the ribs needed to be where they were. What distinguished the keelson from the keel. How the planking worked, each board overlapping like shingles on a roof, creating a hull both strong and flexible. The questions sometimes annoyed him. He'd spent decades working by feel, and here was his son demanding theoretical explanations. But he tried. He'd stop what he was doing, pick up a pencil, sketch a diagram on scrap wood. He'd explain leverage and load distribution in words that were clumsy but always honest.

202:

They made errors. Bob wishes he could tell you some inspiring story about how they were naturals, how everything was perfect. But that's not how it happened.

203:

When things went wrong Bob was devastated. Thirteen, maybe fourteen, old enough to understand what mistakes had cost them. There was wisdom in that Bob wouldn't fully appreciate until decades later, when Bob was managing engineering teams and teaching his own children. The philosophy of the garage—iterative improvement, learning from failure, craftsmanship over speed—became foundational. But at the time, it was simply how things were done. You measured twice and cut once not because someone invented that saying, but because wasting a twelve-dollar piece of plywood mattered when you were a kid working on lemonade sales. You sanded by hand because his father didn't have a power sander.

204:

Something else, something Bob was not proud of. There were days Bob didn't want to be there. Days when his friends played baseball or rode bikes, and Bob was in that garage. Bob resented it. God help him, Bob resented it. That was its own kind of lesson. The universe doesn't negotiate. Materials don't care about your feelings. You can be angry at a piece of wood all day, but it's not going to cut itself. Bob understand now what Bob was learning. Resilience. Responsibility. The understanding that showing up matters more than feeling like it.

207:

One afternoon—Bob must have been fourteen, maybe fifteen—she caught him in the aftermath of a dinner table confrontation. Bob was in the living room, pretending to read, actually just staring at the same page, boiling with that particular teenage rage that has no outlet. She sat down. Didn't say anything for a minute. Just sat there, her hand on his knee. "Your father is a good man," she said finally. "But he doesn't know how to be soft. The war made him hard, and his own father made him harder." Bob wanted to argue. "He's afraid, Robert," she said, using his real name, not the casual "Rob" everyone else used. "Afraid he won't raise you right. Afraid you'll make the mistakes he made. The yelling is fear wearing anger's clothes."

208:

This was her gift to him. Translation. She helped him understand the man who seemed impossible to understand, decoding the emotional language of a generation that had learned to suppress vulnerability. That love could be buried beneath harshness, that discipline could coexist with devotion, that the father who demanded so much did so because he cared too much. Bob didn't believe her then. Bob was fifteen, and fifteen-year-olds know everything, which is to say they know nothing. But the seed was planted. Years later, when Bob had enough distance, Bob realized she'd been right.

209:

She also taught him practical things. If the garage was his father's domain, the kitchen was her laboratory. Not because cooking was women's work—she rejected that—but because independence required competence. "A man who can't feed himself is a man dependent on others," she said, teaching him to make an omelet at twelve. "Your father never learned. You're going to live alone. You need to take care of yourself." She taught him the chemistry of cooking, though she never used that word. How heat transformed proteins. How acids balanced fats. How the Maillard reaction turned flour and butter into gold. She was not a great cook, but she knew how to cook with limited ingredients; money was often tight. When Bob went to college and watched classmates discover they couldn't cook, Bob understood the value. More than survival, cooking taught him patience. A different patience than woodworking, but related. You couldn't rush a braise. You couldn't force bread to rise. You had to work with the ingredients, respect their timelines. His mother's kitchen ran on the same principles as his father's garage: understand your materials, prepare properly, execute with care. She's been gone for years now, but she's still in that kitchen. Still teaching.

211:

Watching his parents together, Bob began to see their marriage as a kind of complex system where two very different people complemented each other. His father provided and protected, fixed what broke, handled the physical world. His mother managed, planned, maintained the emotional infrastructure. She moderated him. When his temper flared, she intervened—not by contradicting him, which would escalate things, but by redirection. By the quiet authority she had built through years of competence. "Don't judge your father by his worst moments," she told him once. "Judge him by his consistency. By what he provides. By the fact that he never leaves, never gives up, never stops working for this family. He doesn't know how to say he loves you. But he shows it every day."

213:

"I don't want you to be like your father," she said once, surprising him. They were folding laundry—his junior year of high school—and Bob had said something about never yelling at his kids the way he yelled at him. "I want you to be like yourself. Take his good parts—his work ethic, his loyalty, his ability to make things. Leave behind the parts that hurt. That's how generations get better. Not by copying, but by selecting." This was evolution, she explained. Cultural evolution, family evolution, the slow process by which each generation improves on the last. It required awareness, which his father lacked, and intention, which she possessed in abundance.

214:

Bob thought about that conversation a lot. About what Bob kept from his parents and what Bob discarded. Bob kept the work ethic. The belief that showing up matters. The understanding that love is a verb, not a feeling. Bob discarded the yelling. The rigidity. The belief that obedience was more important than understanding. His mother would be proud, Bob thought. Or she'd just nod and say, "Good. Now help me fold these sheets."

216:

The building wasn't the only education happening in the garage. His father had an old radio—tube-type, pre-transistor, probably from the late '40s—and Bob learned how it worked. Invisible signals pulled from the air, transformed by glowing filaments and magnetic coils, emerging as voices and music from a paper cone. How was that even possible? "Electricity is just organized lightning," he explained, showing him the resistor color codes. Black, brown, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, gray, white. Zero through nine. Bob memorized that sequence like the alphabet before knowing what reading was for. His brothers never seemed interested.

217:

He showed him how to solder without cold joints. How to trace a circuit from power supply to output. How to use a multimeter, the needle dancing as you found the right range. "It wants to get from here to there," he said, pointing at the schematic. "Your job is to give it a path and control how much gets through." Bob built his own projects. A crystal radio needing no batteries, pulling power from the radio waves themselves—a wooden box with a coil of wire and a crystal detector, and if you tuned the slider just right, you could pull in Detroit clear as a bell on a good night. A simple amplifier from plans in a library book. An electric motor from wire, magnets, and a battery—Faraday's laws made visible. Each success led to greater ambition. Each failure led to deeper understanding. The garage became his laboratory, his sanctuary, the place where theory met practice.

218:

"You've got good hands," he said once. High praise. In the garage, curiosity was valued. Understanding the why mattered as much as the result. Bob didn't know it then, but Bob was building more than radios or motors. Bob was building a way of being in the world. The confidence that Bob could figure things out, take something broken and make it whole, start with nothing and end with something that worked. That confidence would carry him through engineering school, through career setbacks, through the inevitable crises of adult life. Built plank by plank, wire by wire, mistake by mistake.

220:

Working alongside his father, Bob began to see the man beneath the Navy veteran. Beneath the authoritarian parent. Bob learned how he'd wanted to be an architect, but the war derailed those plans. How he'd met his mother during a chance encounter and known within minutes she was the one. How terrified he'd been at becoming a father, certain he'd repeat the mistakes of his own harsh upbringing—his own father a womanizer and gambler on the road as a train engineer.

221:

"I swore I'd be different," he said one evening, fitting a breasthook into the bow while Bob held it steady. The curved piece of wood reinforced the joint where the bow timbers met; it had to be perfect or the whole front of the boat would be weak. "Then you were born and I had no idea what I was doing. So I fell back on what I knew. The Navy way." He didn't apologize. That wasn't his way. But the admission hung in the air between them—an acknowledgment that the man in the house and the man in the garage were not the same person. Bob was seventeen, old enough to understand complexity but young enough to still want simple answers. And in that moment Bob understood: sometimes love isn't about the words. It's about showing up. About teaching someone to build. About trusting them with dangerous tools and the space to make mistakes. He never said "I love you" much. But he was there. Every Saturday. For years. Teaching him what he knew. Letting him become someone he couldn't be.

223:

By the time Bob was fourteen, Bob had outgrown the role of assistant. Bob had his own projects now, his own sense of what Bob wanted to build.

225:

His brother and Bob launched it on a cool spring morning. The boat wasn't perfect—it showed the evolution of his skills over the year-long build, the forward planks fitting better than the aft ones, mistakes preserved in wood and epoxy. But they had sealed every joint, sanded every rough edge, painted the hull white. It moved through the lake with a grace that seemed impossible for something built by amateurs in a suburban garage.

226:

His brother rowed first, testing the trim, checking for leaks. Then they raised the sail. Bob settled onto the rear seat and felt the boat respond to his weight, becoming an extension of his intentions. It creaked. Water lapped against the hull. The wind caught the canvas and the boat leaned into it, and Bob understood, truly understood for the first time, what creation felt like. This was something that had existed only in a magazine drawing, then in a pile of lumber and fasteners, and now—against all odds—it was moving across real water, doing what they had designed it to do.

228:

They never used the boat much after that. It sat in the garage, then a storage shed, later sold to someone who never knew the history in its imperfect seams. The point was never the boat. The point was the building. When Bob look back on that spring morning, what Bob remembered most is his father's face as they pushed off from the dock. His eyes bright with an emotion Bob would later recognize as love. Not the demanding love of expectation, but the generous love of seeing someone you care about become who they were meant to be.

230:

High school brought new interests. Girls. A part-time job at the local TV repair shop. The looming decisions about college that would carry him away. But the foundation had been laid. In the garage, Bob had learned Bob was capable of building complex things from raw materials. That knowledge could be acquired through persistence, skill through repetition, mistakes were tuition paid toward mastery. Bob had learned his father contained multitudes—not just the authoritarian figure, but a craftsman, a teacher, a man with his own disappointments who had tried, in his imperfect way, to give his son the tools for a better life. Years later, when Bob brought his own children to the garage, his father no longer had the patience for tutoring beginners. The grandchildren never saw the best in him. That made him sad, but it also made him grateful for what Bob had gotten when the timing was right.

231:

When Bob had his own children, Bob tried to recreate this magic. Bob built a workbench. Bought tools and lumber. Invited his son to build together. It wasn't the same—they had different interests, different paths. But the principle held. The time together mattered. The transmission of knowledge and confidence, the joy of making something real with your own hands—that still worked, even across generations.

232:

Bob sometimes wonders if his father knew, in some wordless way, that they were building more than boats and airplanes. That the real project was the son beside him, learning to trust his own competence, preparing to row out into waters his father would never navigate. The garage door still opened on those evenings, spilling light into the suburban dark, the smell of sawdust and oil drifting out like incense. Inside, two people bent to their work, passing time together in the shared language of making, building something that would outlast them both.

234:

The skills learned in that garage—the patience to measure twice, the courage to fail and rebuild, the understanding that invisible forces could be harnessed to do extraordinary things—would soon find an outlet far beyond anything Bob could have imagined. The Space Race had begun, and a boy who had learned to build models and troubleshoot radios was about to discover that his hands could help build something that would reach for the stars themselves.

236:

In 1965, young Bob was not just a boy with a dream; he was a boy with a blueprint. His early forays into rocketry were humble, starting with simple solid-fueled rockets that he and his friends would launch in open fields. These rockets were straightforward, powered by a blend of powdered metals and oxidizers. The thrill of watching these homemade marvels ascend into the sky was a formative experience, each launch etching what neuroscientists call an “episodic memory” into his young mind.

237:

As Bob entered his teenage years, his ambitions soared alongside his rockets. He graduated from solid-fueled rockets to more advanced liquid-fueled models. Unlike their solid counterparts, liquid-fueled rockets offered greater control over thrust and could be shut down or throttled as needed. They were more complex, requiring a deeper understanding of engineering principles, but the payoff was a rocket that could reach higher altitudes with more precise control.

239:

Not all flights were smooth. One sunny afternoon, a launch turned into a cautionary tale. The rocket malfunctioned; a tailfin broke off, sending it crashing into a neighbor’s garage roof. Panic surged through Bob and his friends as they saw flames and smoke. Racing against time, they managed to repair the damage before the homeowner returned, their hearts pounding in their chests. This incident was a wake-up call, adding a layer of caution to their adventures and serving as a constant reminder of the responsibilities that come with passion.

242:

Also in 1965, Bob’s life took another transformative turn when he joined the Boy Scouts of America. It was not just an extracurricular activity; it was a rite of passage, a crucible of character-building, and a forge for friendships that would last a lifetime.

243:

Bob was immediately captivated by the Scouts’ ethos of community, self-reliance, and respect for nature. The first skill he learned was orienteering, the art of navigating through unfamiliar terrain with just a map and compass. This was not merely a practical skill; it was a metaphor for life itself. Bob realized that with the right tools and knowledge, one could navigate through any of life’s challenges. This lesson became an episodic memory—a specific event that would shape his decision-making in the years to come.

244:

Bob was a dedicated member of the Boy Scouts, and his experiences in the organization had a profound impact on his life. He earned over thirty merit badges, but two in particular stood out: the hiking merit badge and the Polar Bear badge.

245:

To earn the hiking merit badge, Bob had to complete two twelve-mile hikes and one twenty-five-mile hike. This was a challenging task for a thirteen-year-old, but Bob was determined to achieve it. After completing the first two hikes, Bob had destroyed his shoes, and his family was going through a difficult financial period. His mother managed to find him a new pair of shoes that were two sizes too big. Bob made it work by wearing three pairs of socks and embarked on the twenty-five-mile hike. It took him all day to complete, walking across Jackson County alone, taking breaks and having lunch along the way. Despite the pain and persistence required, Bob remembers it as a huge accomplishment.

246:

The second badge that shaped Bob was the Polar Bear Badge. To earn it, he had to spend twenty-four hours camping outdoors in temperatures below thirty-two degrees Fahrenheit. The weekend Bob attempted the badge, the night temperature dipped below zero. Five boys attempted the badge, but the four others did not want to do it with Bob, so he was left to build his own shelter alone. The other boys built a debris shelter, but Bob knew he needed to do something different if he wanted to survive the night. He thought hard and built a lean-to shelter, lining the inside with aluminum cooking foil. He then built a fire, focusing the heat on his sleeping bag. Bob stayed up all night, waking every couple of hours to add more wood to the fire. By six the next morning, the scoutmaster came to check on him, and Bob was doing fine—though he was almost out of firewood.

251:

The summer before tenth grade, Bob's father announced it was time his son learned what work actually meant. Not the abstract work of school, not the weekend projects in the garage, but the clock-punching, customer-serving, paycheck-earning reality that occupied most of adult life. He had arranged a job at Hendricks TV & Electronics, a small repair shop that smelled of solder flux and ozone and the particular mustiness of vacuum tubes past their prime.

255:

Bob spent the next ten minutes demonstrating what he knew—how to tin an iron, how to heat the joint rather than the solder, how to create that bright concave fillet that meant a good connection. Mr. Hendricks watched without comment, then handed him a basket of vacuum tubes.

257:

The job paid $1.25 an hour, minimum wage, but the education was worth far more. Bob spent that summer and the two that followed driving around town doing pickup and delivery alongside an older worker, learning the applied electronics that would form the foundation of his career. He learned to read schematic diagrams—those intricate maps of electron flow that turned abstract symbols into working circuits. He learned to trace signals through televisions and radios, to identify failure points by symptom, to repair rather than replace because customers couldn't afford new sets.

258:

It was in that shop, surrounded by the glow of testing equipment and the smell of hot solder, that Bob first understood the difference between school knowledge and real knowledge. School taught you principles. The shop taught you what to do when the principles failed.

259:

Bob's first encounter with a real computer came not in the shop, but through a teacher. Dr. Richardson taught mathematics, and Bob noticed the man carried a textbook titled Introduction to Digital Computers.

260:

"You interested in that sort of thing?" Dr. Richardson asked, watching Bob eye the book.

263:

Bob went the following Saturday. The computer filled a room—cabinets of transistors and magnetic core memory, spinning tape drives that sounded like sewing machines on amphetamines. Dr. Richardson showed him how to punch cards, how to write simple programs in raw assembly code, how the machine translated human instructions into the binary language of on-off switches and logic gates.

265:

That afternoon, Bob decided he would be an electrical engineer. Not a casual ambition, but a certainty that settled into his bones the way solder settled into a joint. He wanted to work with these machines, these thinking engines that were transforming the world. He wanted to understand capabilities that hadn't been imagined yet. The room-sized computer before him had less computing power than a modern pocket calculator—but to Bob, standing in that fluorescent-lit classroom, it was the most magnificent thing he had ever seen.

267:

Bob's first car was a 1962 Chrysler Valiant, powder blue, with a mind of its own. The heater worked only when it wanted to, which in Michigan meant Bob spent most of the winter driving with the windows cracked to keep the windshield from fogging. The manual gearshift had its own agenda, sometimes finding third when he reached for first, sometimes refusing to find any gear at all until he'd pumped the clutch three times and said the right incantation.

268:

His parents bought it with the understanding that Bob would pay them back. He earned the money working weekends at Hendricks TV & Electronics, and every dollar he handed over felt like a declaration of independence. The Valiant represented something more than transportation—it was the first tangible evidence that he could provide for himself. He remembered driving to the lake with his friends, the wind in their hair, the radio blasting whatever station they could pick up. They had no destination, not really. They just drove. Followed roads they'd never taken, discovered places they'd never known existed, pulled over at random diners to eat french fries and feel alive.

270:

Bob's high school didn't offer computer classes—they barely had functioning typewriters—but it had a physics teacher named Mr. Kovacs who recognized something in the quiet student who sat in the front row and asked questions that went beyond the curriculum.

function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

REPLACE MODE (mode='replace', default): find a unique string and replace it. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, path, old_string, new_string.
PATCH MODE (mode='patch'): apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, patch.

mode.description: Edit mode. 'replace' (default): requires path + old_string + new_string. 'patch': requires patch content only.

path.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. File path to edit.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits. Auto-runs syntax checks on .py/.json/.yaml/.toml and other linted languages; only NEW errors introduced by this write are surfaced (pre-existing errors are filtered out).

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file
